topic_brief.title: No-till vs conventional tillage effects on crop yield
topic_brief.research_question: Does no-till management affect crop yield compared to conventional tillage, and how does this vary by crop type and climate?
topic_brief.population_description: Crop plants grown in field experiments comparing tillage systems
topic_brief.intervention_description: No-till or zero-till management (seeds planted directly into undisturbed soil)
topic_brief.comparator_description: Conventional tillage (moldboard plow, disk, chisel, or other inversion/intensive tillage)
topic_brief.outcome_description: Crop grain yield per unit area
tc_confusion_warnings: Treatment is NO-TILL (less disturbance), Control is CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (more disturbance)
Reduced tillage is NOT no-till - if both exist, compare no-till vs conventional
Some papers have 3+ tillage levels - extract the no-till vs most intensive tillage comparison
Strip-till is intermediate - do not include as no-till unless paper explicitly calls it no-till
Long-term trials may show different effects in early vs late years - extract each year separately
extraction_priorities: 1. CRITICAL: Extract EVERY crop-year-site combination separately
2. Treatment = NO-TILL; Control = CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (most intensive tillage in the study)
3. If multiple crops tested, extract EACH crop vs control
4. If reduced tillage AND no-till both present, extract no-till vs conventional (not reduced vs conventional)
5. Get variance (SE/SD/LSD) and sample size (n)
6. Record crop species and years since no-till adoption
7. Record residue management practice
topic_brief.benchmark_notes: Overall -5.7%; Wheat -2.6%; Maize -7.6%; Rice -7.5%; Soybean +0.3%; Oilseed rape -9.0%

row.title: Study of fuel consumption in three tillage methods
row.authors: Akbarnia A., Farhani F.
row.treatment_description: No-tillage using direct drill planter (Ozdoken Model 2007), working depth 20 cm, no soil disturbance
row.control_description: Maximum (conventional) tillage: moldboard plow + tandem disk harrow (3 stages) + leveler + seed planter, working depth 30 cm
row.notes: Yield significantly different between tillage systems (ANOVA F=9.60, p<0.05). Duncan's test groups max. tillage in class 1 and no-tillage in class 2, confirming significant difference. MSE=0.07125 computed from ANOVA error SS=0.285 with df=4 (pooled across all 3 tillage systems). Pooled SD=sqrt(MSE)=0.267 t/ha. Farm previously used for corn, causing soil compaction and hard pan which authors note negatively affected no-till planter performance. Paper primarily focused on fuel consumption, yield is secondary outcome.

moderators.mod_residue_management: retained (trash remained on surface for no-till)

row.title: A regionally-adapted implementation of conservation agriculture delivers rapid improvements to soil properties associated with crop yield stability
row.authors: Alwyn Williams, Nicholas R. Jordan, Richard G. Smith, Mitchell C. Hunter, Melanie Kammerer, Daniel A. Kane, Roger T. Koide, Adam S. Davis
row.treatment_description: Ridge tillage (reduced tillage, NOT no-till) across 4 US states (IL, MI, MN, PA), 2012-2015, maize-soybean rotation
row.control_description: Chisel plough (conventional tillage) across 4 US states, 2012-2015, maize-soybean rotation
row.notes: CRITICAL: This paper compares RIDGE TILLAGE (reduced tillage) vs CHISEL PLOUGH (conventional tillage). Ridge tillage is NOT no-till — the paper explicitly calls it 'reduced tillage'. The PICO definition requires no-till vs conventional tillage. This observation may NOT qualify for inclusion. Absolute mean yields are not reported in the main text; only the difference is given: ridge tillage yielded 331 kg/ha less than chisel plough across all site-years (t1,215=2.00, P=0.047). The yield data are in supplementary Figure S4 which is not available in this PDF. 4 replicate blocks per site × 4 sites = 16 plot-level replicates per treatment (pooled across cover crop treatments and years).

tc_confusion_warnings: Treatment is NO-TILL (less disturbance), Control is CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (more disturbance)

7. Record residue management practice

topic_brief.outcome_description: Crop grain yield per unit area
tc_confusion_warnings: Treatment is NO-TILL (less disturbance), Control is CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (more disturbance)
Reduced tillage is NOT no-till - if both exist, compare no-till vs conventional
Some papers have 3+ tillage levels - extract the no-till vs most intensive tillage comparison
Strip-till is intermediate - do not include as no-till unless paper explicitly calls it no-till
Long-term trials may show different effects in early vs late years - extract each year separately
extraction_priorities: 1. CRITICAL: Extract EVERY crop-year-site combination separately
2. Treatment = NO-TILL; Control = CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (most intensive tillage in the study)
3. If multiple crops tested, extract EACH crop vs control
4. If reduced tillage AND no-till both present, extract no-till vs conventional (not reduced vs conventional)
5. Get variance (SE/SD/LSD) and sample size (n)
6. Record crop species and years since no-till adoption
7. Record residue management practice
topic_brief.benchmark_notes: Overall -5.7%; Wheat -2.6%; Maize -7.6%; Rice -7.5%; Soybean +0.3%; Oilseed rape -9.0%

row.title: Conservation Tillage and Pesticide Use in the Cornbelt
row.authors: Keith O. Fuglie
row.journal: Journal of Agricultural and Applied Economics
row.treatment_description: No-till (zero tillage, direct seeding)
row.control_description: Conventional tillage with moldboard plow
row.notes: NOT A FIELD TRIAL — this is an econometric analysis of cross-sectional survey data (1,425 Cornbelt corn fields). No raw treatment/control mean yields are reported. The yield effect of no-till is estimated via 2SLS regression coefficient: Prob(no till) = -29.059 bu/acre (t=-3.291, p<0.05). Mean sample yield = 140.14 bu/acre (SD=40.59). The regression controls for farm size, irrigation, rotation, soil quality, soil erosion, soil leaching potential, climate (season length, rainfall), state, herbicide use, insecticide use, and fertilizer use. The coefficient suggests no-till reduces corn yield by ~29 bu/acre relative to conventional tillage, but this is model-estimated, not a simple mean comparison. Elasticity of corn yield w.r.t. Prob(no till) = -0.043 (Table 7, significant at 10%). This paper may not be suitable for inclusion in a standard meta-analysis requiring treatment and control group means.

moderators.mod_study_type: cross-sectional farm survey (Area Studies Survey, USDA)

topic_brief.intervention_description: No-till or zero-till management (seeds planted directly into undisturbed soil)
topic_brief.comparator_description: Conventional tillage (moldboard plow, disk, chisel, or other inversion/intensive tillage)
topic_brief.outcome_description: Crop grain yield per unit area
tc_confusion_warnings: Treatment is NO-TILL (less disturbance), Control is CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (more disturbance)
Reduced tillage is NOT no-till - if both exist, compare no-till vs conventional
Some papers have 3+ tillage levels - extract the no-till vs most intensive tillage comparison
Strip-till is intermediate - do not include as no-till unless paper explicitly calls it no-till
Long-term trials may show different effects in early vs late years - extract each year separately
extraction_priorities: 1. CRITICAL: Extract EVERY crop-year-site combination separately
2. Treatment = NO-TILL; Control = CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (most intensive tillage in the study)
3. If multiple crops tested, extract EACH crop vs control
4. If reduced tillage AND no-till both present, extract no-till vs conventional (not reduced vs conventional)
5. Get variance (SE/SD/LSD) and sample size (n)
6. Record crop species and years since no-till adoption
7. Record residue management practice
topic_brief.benchmark_notes: Overall -5.7%; Wheat -2.6%; Maize -7.6%; Rice -7.5%; Soybean +0.3%; Oilseed rape -9.0%

row.title: Shallow non-inversion tillage in organic farming maintains crop yields and increases soil C stocks: a meta-analysis
row.authors: Cooper J, Baranski M, Stewart G, Nobel-de Lange M, Bàrberi P, Fließbach A, Peigné J, Berner A, Brock C, Casagrande M, Crowley O, David C, De Vliegher A, Döring TF, Dupont A, Entz M, Grosse M, Haase T, Halde C, Hammerl V, Huiting H, Leithold G, Messmer M, Schloter M, Sukkel W, van der Heijden MGA, Willekens K, Wittwer R, Mäder P

Unweighted analysis. This is the overall effect across all reduced tillage classes vs deep inversion.

row.title: Effects of different management practices on the soil-water balance and crop yield for improved dryland farming in the Chinese Loess Plateau

row.treatment_description: No-till with mulch (NT): 30 cm stubble retained, straw returned, direct sowing by hand

topic_brief.title: No-till vs conventional tillage effects on crop yield
topic_brief.research_question: Does no-till management affect crop yield compared to conventional tillage, and how does this vary by crop type and climate?
topic_brief.population_description: Crop plants grown in field experiments comparing tillage systems
topic_brief.intervention_description: No-till or zero-till management (seeds planted directly into undisturbed soil)
topic_brief.comparator_description: Conventional tillage (moldboard plow, disk, chisel, or other inversion/intensive tillage)
topic_brief.outcome_description: Crop grain yield per unit area
tc_confusion_warnings: Treatment is NO-TILL (less disturbance), Control is CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (more disturbance)
Reduced tillage is NOT no-till - if both exist, compare no-till vs conventional
Some papers have 3+ tillage levels - extract the no-till vs most intensive tillage comparison
Strip-till is intermediate - do not include as no-till unless paper explicitly calls it no-till
Long-term trials may show different effects in early vs late years - extract each year separately
extraction_priorities: 1. CRITICAL: Extract EVERY crop-year-site combination separately
2. Treatment = NO-TILL; Control = CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (most intensive tillage in the study)
3. If multiple crops tested, extract EACH crop vs control
4. If reduced tillage AND no-till both present, extract no-till vs conventional (not reduced vs conventional)
5. Get variance (SE/SD/LSD) and sample size (n)
6. Record crop species and years since no-till adoption
7. Record residue management practice
topic_brief.benchmark_notes: Overall -5.7%; Wheat -2.6%; Maize -7.6%; Rice -7.5%; Soybean +0.3%; Oilseed rape -9.0%

topic_brief.title: No-till vs conventional tillage effects on crop yield
topic_brief.research_question: Does no-till management affect crop yield compared to conventional tillage, and how does this vary by crop type and climate?
topic_brief.population_description: Crop plants grown in field experiments comparing tillage systems
topic_brief.intervention_description: No-till or zero-till management (seeds planted directly into undisturbed soil)
topic_brief.comparator_description: Conventional tillage (moldboard plow, disk, chisel, or other inversion/intensive tillage)
topic_brief.outcome_description: Crop grain yield per unit area
tc_confusion_warnings: Treatment is NO-TILL (less disturbance), Control is CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (more disturbance)
Reduced tillage is NOT no-till - if both exist, compare no-till vs conventional
Some papers have 3+ tillage levels - extract the no-till vs most intensive tillage comparison
Strip-till is intermediate - do not include as no-till unless paper explicitly calls it no-till
Long-term trials may show different effects in early vs late years - extract each year separately
extraction_priorities: 1. CRITICAL: Extract EVERY crop-year-site combination separately
2. Treatment = NO-TILL; Control = CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (most intensive tillage in the study)
3. If multiple crops tested, extract EACH crop vs control
4. If reduced tillage AND no-till both present, extract no-till vs conventional (not reduced vs conventional)
5. Get variance (SE/SD/LSD) and sample size (n)
6. Record crop species and years since no-till adoption
7. Record residue management practice
topic_brief.benchmark_notes: Overall -5.7%; Wheat -2.6%; Maize -7.6%; Rice -7.5%; Soybean +0.3%; Oilseed rape -9.0%

topic_brief.title: No-till vs conventional tillage effects on crop yield
topic_brief.research_question: Does no-till management affect crop yield compared to conventional tillage, and how does this vary by crop type and climate?
topic_brief.population_description: Crop plants grown in field experiments comparing tillage systems
topic_brief.intervention_description: No-till or zero-till management (seeds planted directly into undisturbed soil)
topic_brief.comparator_description: Conventional tillage (moldboard plow, disk, chisel, or other inversion/intensive tillage)
topic_brief.outcome_description: Crop grain yield per unit area
tc_confusion_warnings: Treatment is NO-TILL (less disturbance), Control is CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (more disturbance)
Reduced tillage is NOT no-till - if both exist, compare no-till vs conventional
Some papers have 3+ tillage levels - extract the no-till vs most intensive tillage comparison
Strip-till is intermediate - do not include as no-till unless paper explicitly calls it no-till
Long-term trials may show different effects in early vs late years - extract each year separately
extraction_priorities: 1. CRITICAL: Extract EVERY crop-year-site combination separately
2. Treatment = NO-TILL; Control = CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (most intensive tillage in the study)
3. If multiple crops tested, extract EACH crop vs control
4. If reduced tillage AND no-till both present, extract no-till vs conventional (not reduced vs conventional)
5. Get variance (SE/SD/LSD) and sample size (n)
6. Record crop species and years since no-till adoption
7. Record residue management practice
topic_brief.benchmark_notes: Overall -5.7%; Wheat -2.6%; Maize -7.6%; Rice -7.5%; Soybean +0.3%; Oilseed rape -9.0%

row.treatment_description: Reduced tillage (RT): unpuddled transplanted rice, land prepared with Power Tiller Operated Seeder (PTOS) with 2 passes, no puddling or leveling
row.control_description: Conventional tillage (CT): puddled transplanted rice, 6 passes with power tiller plus soil puddling and leveling
row.notes: Main effect of tillage averaged across 3 irrigation methods (Flood, AWD, Sprinkler). n=9 per tillage level (3 irrigation x 3 reps). Paper calls this 'reduced tillage' (unpuddled) not 'no-till' or 'zero-till'; RT involves 2 passes with PTOS without puddling. Tillage x irrigation interaction was not significant for yield. CV=3.29%. LSD(0.05)=0.19 t/ha.

moderators.mod_irrigation: averaged across flood, AWD, and sprinkler irrigation

topic_brief.title: No-till vs conventional tillage effects on crop yield
topic_brief.research_question: Does no-till management affect crop yield compared to conventional tillage, and how does this vary by crop type and climate?
topic_brief.population_description: Crop plants grown in field experiments comparing tillage systems
topic_brief.intervention_description: No-till or zero-till management (seeds planted directly into undisturbed soil)
topic_brief.comparator_description: Conventional tillage (moldboard plow, disk, chisel, or other inversion/intensive tillage)
topic_brief.outcome_description: Crop grain yield per unit area
tc_confusion_warnings: Treatment is NO-TILL (less disturbance), Control is CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (more disturbance)
Reduced tillage is NOT no-till - if both exist, compare no-till vs conventional
Some papers have 3+ tillage levels - extract the no-till vs most intensive tillage comparison
Strip-till is intermediate - do not include as no-till unless paper explicitly calls it no-till
Long-term trials may show different effects in early vs late years - extract each year separately
extraction_priorities: 1. CRITICAL: Extract EVERY crop-year-site combination separately
2. Treatment = NO-TILL; Control = CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (most intensive tillage in the study)
3. If multiple crops tested, extract EACH crop vs control
4. If reduced tillage AND no-till both present, extract no-till vs conventional (not reduced vs conventional)
5. Get variance (SE/SD/LSD) and sample size (n)
6. Record crop species and years since no-till adoption
7. Record residue management practice
topic_brief.benchmark_notes: Overall -5.7%; Wheat -2.6%; Maize -7.6%; Rice -7.5%; Soybean +0.3%; Oilseed rape -9.0%

row.title: Are No-Till Herbicide-Free Systems Possible? A Simulation Study
row.authors: Nathalie Colbach, Stéphane Cordeau
row.treatment_description: Tillage-free (all tillage operations deleted from recorded cropping systems, no other changes)
row.control_description: Recorded cropping systems (with tillage as practiced)
row.notes: SIMULATION STUDY — NOT empirical field data. Treatment mean calculated as 130738 − 44999 = 85739 MJ/ha. Values are averages across 395 simulated cropping systems × 30 years × 10 weather repetitions (118,500 data points per series). Yield is in MJ/ha (energy content), not directly convertible to t/ha without crop-specific energy values. The −34% effect is primarily weed-mediated (see potential yield observation showing only −2% without weeds). No experimental replication — n reflects number of simulated systems, not field replicates. No per-group variance reported for these yield values.

row.title: Are No-Till Herbicide-Free Systems Possible? A Simulation Study
row.authors: Nathalie Colbach, Stéphane Cordeau
row.outcome: Grain yield loss due to weeds
row.treatment_description: NoTill — all tillage operations deleted from recorded cropping systems without other changes
row.control_description: Standard — recorded cropping systems simulated without modification
row.notes: SIMULATION STUDY. CAUTION: This outcome is yield LOSS (higher value = worse crop performance), not yield itself. The no-till treatment had 48.5% yield loss vs 27.5% for standard tillage. Blue diamonds in Figure 3 show means; letters A, B, C indicate significant differences at p=0.05. The effect_pct of +76.4% means yield LOSS increased by 76% when tillage was deleted. For a meta-analysis of YIELD (not yield loss), use the Table 3 actual yield observation instead. Also: NoHerbicides treatment showed 44.9% yield loss (letter B).

row.title: Weed dynamics and productivity of wheat (Triticum aestivum) under various tillage and weed management practices
row.authors: Parmeswar Dayal, Arun Kumar, Shashank Tyagi, Ravikesh Kumar Pal, Bal Manohar, Shivani Ranjan, Sumit Sow
row.treatment_description: Zero tillage (ZT), direct seeding with zero-till ferti-cum-seed drill, rice residues retained on surface
row.control_description: Conventional tillage (CT), standard tillage practices
row.notes: Treatment mean (40.08 q/ha) explicitly stated in text. Control mean (~34 q/ha) estimated from Figure 1 bar chart. SE values (~3 q/ha each) estimated from figure error bars with low precision. Paper has T1/T2 label inconsistency: methodology defines T1=ZT and T2=CT, but weed density/biomass data in Table 1 show T2 with lower weed counts, which the text attributes to zero tillage. However, the yield text unambiguously states 'Zero tillage produced a maximum yield of 40.08 q/ha' matching T1 as the taller bar in Figure 1. Number of replications not stated (likely 3 based on typical Indian agricultural experimental designs). LSD used for mean comparisons (P=0.05) but LSD value for yield not reported. The positive effect (+17.9%) for no-till contradicts the expected negative direction but is consistent with rice-wheat systems in the Indo-Gangetic Plains where ZT with residue retention often increases wheat yield. Single-season study (2021-22). Weed management was a subplot factor with 9 levels; yield data reported only as tillage main-effect means averaged across weed management practices.

moderators.mod_residue_management: retained (rice residues on surface under ZT)

row.control_description: Conventional intensive tillage (C-IT), legume cover crop (hairy vetch)
row.notes: Estimated from Figure 1 bar chart. Legume cover crop before maize = hairy vetch (Vicia villosa). Text states legume cover crop (hairy vetch) increased maize yield by 61% (O-RT), 27% (O-IT), 14% (C-NT), 8% (C-IT) vs bare fallow. Legume cover crop effect on maize was significant in all systems except C-IT. Hairy vetch produced the most biomass before maize (2.4 t/ha). Approximately 89% of N in hairy vetch was from biological N fixation (94 kg N/ha additional N input).

topic_brief.comparator_description: Conventional tillage (moldboard plow, disk, chisel, or other inversion/intensive tillage)
topic_brief.outcome_description: Crop grain yield per unit area
tc_confusion_warnings: Treatment is NO-TILL (less disturbance), Control is CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (more disturbance)
Reduced tillage is NOT no-till - if both exist, compare no-till vs conventional
Some papers have 3+ tillage levels - extract the no-till vs most intensive tillage comparison
Strip-till is intermediate - do not include as no-till unless paper explicitly calls it no-till
Long-term trials may show different effects in early vs late years - extract each year separately
extraction_priorities: 1. CRITICAL: Extract EVERY crop-year-site combination separately
2. Treatment = NO-TILL; Control = CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (most intensive tillage in the study)
3. If multiple crops tested, extract EACH crop vs control
4. If reduced tillage AND no-till both present, extract no-till vs conventional (not reduced vs conventional)
5. Get variance (SE/SD/LSD) and sample size (n)
6. Record crop species and years since no-till adoption
7. Record residue management practice
topic_brief.benchmark_notes: Overall -5.7%; Wheat -2.6%; Maize -7.6%; Rice -7.5%; Soybean +0.3%; Oilseed rape -9.0%

topic_brief.population_description: Crop plants grown in field experiments comparing tillage systems
topic_brief.intervention_description: No-till or zero-till management (seeds planted directly into undisturbed soil)
topic_brief.comparator_description: Conventional tillage (moldboard plow, disk, chisel, or other inversion/intensive tillage)
topic_brief.outcome_description: Crop grain yield per unit area
tc_confusion_warnings: Treatment is NO-TILL (less disturbance), Control is CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (more disturbance)
Reduced tillage is NOT no-till - if both exist, compare no-till vs conventional
Some papers have 3+ tillage levels - extract the no-till vs most intensive tillage comparison
Strip-till is intermediate - do not include as no-till unless paper explicitly calls it no-till
Long-term trials may show different effects in early vs late years - extract each year separately
extraction_priorities: 1. CRITICAL: Extract EVERY crop-year-site combination separately
2. Treatment = NO-TILL; Control = CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (most intensive tillage in the study)
3. If multiple crops tested, extract EACH crop vs control
4. If reduced tillage AND no-till both present, extract no-till vs conventional (not reduced vs conventional)
5. Get variance (SE/SD/LSD) and sample size (n)
6. Record crop species and years since no-till adoption
7. Record residue management practice
topic_brief.benchmark_notes: Overall -5.7%; Wheat -2.6%; Maize -7.6%; Rice -7.5%; Soybean +0.3%; Oilseed rape -9.0%

row.title: Impact of Cover Crop Species on Soil Physical Properties, Cotton Yield, and Profitability
row.authors: Savana D. Denton, Darrin M. Dodds, L. Jason Krutz, Jac J. Varco, Jeffrey Gore, Brian Mills, and Tyson B. Raper
row.treatment_description: Cereal rye cover crop, conventional tillage
row.control_description: Winter fallow, conventional tillage
row.notes: PICO MISMATCH: This paper does NOT compare no-till vs conventional tillage. ALL plots are conventionally tilled (disked + bedded). Comparison is cover crop vs winter fallow within conventional tillage. SE from PROC MIXED LSMEANS pooled across 3 site-years (Starkville 2017, Starkville 2018, Tribbett 2017) and 2 irrigation levels. n=4 reps per site-year; effective n for pooled LSMEAN is larger. Cover crop effect on yield was NS (p>=0.2257).

moderators.mod_residue_management: cover crop rolled down before planting
moderators.mod_crop_rotation: cotton monoculture with winter cover crop

topic_brief.intervention_description: No-till or zero-till management (seeds planted directly into undisturbed soil)
topic_brief.comparator_description: Conventional tillage (moldboard plow, disk, chisel, or other inversion/intensive tillage)
topic_brief.outcome_description: Crop grain yield per unit area
tc_confusion_warnings: Treatment is NO-TILL (less disturbance), Control is CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (more disturbance)
Reduced tillage is NOT no-till - if both exist, compare no-till vs conventional
Some papers have 3+ tillage levels - extract the no-till vs most intensive tillage comparison
Strip-till is intermediate - do not include as no-till unless paper explicitly calls it no-till
Long-term trials may show different effects in early vs late years - extract each year separately
extraction_priorities: 1. CRITICAL: Extract EVERY crop-year-site combination separately
2. Treatment = NO-TILL; Control = CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (most intensive tillage in the study)
3. If multiple crops tested, extract EACH crop vs control
4. If reduced tillage AND no-till both present, extract no-till vs conventional (not reduced vs conventional)
5. Get variance (SE/SD/LSD) and sample size (n)
6. Record crop species and years since no-till adoption
7. Record residue management practice
topic_brief.benchmark_notes: Overall -5.7%; Wheat -2.6%; Maize -7.6%; Rice -7.5%; Soybean +0.3%; Oilseed rape -9.0%

row.title: Energy Requirements and Performance of Different Soil Tillage Systems on the Yield of Maize Crop
row.authors: Shafique Q Memon, Nasima Arshad
row.journal: Advances in Crop Science and Technology
row.treatment_description: Zero tillage (direct drill, no soil disturbance)
row.control_description: Deep tillage (sub soiler + moldboard plow, most intensive tillage)

row.notes: This observation is ZT vs DT (no-till vs most intensive tillage in the study). Deep tillage uses sub soiler + moldboard plow which is the most intensive tillage in this 3-treatment study. topic_brief.population_description: Crop plants grown in field experiments comparing tillage systems
topic_brief.intervention_description: No-till or zero-till management (seeds planted directly into undisturbed soil)

topic_brief.outcome_description: Crop grain yield per unit area
tc_confusion_warnings: Treatment is NO-TILL (less disturbance), Control is CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (more disturbance)
Reduced tillage is NOT no-till - if both exist, compare no-till vs conventional
Some papers have 3+ tillage levels - extract the no-till vs most intensive tillage comparison
Strip-till is intermediate - do not include as no-till unless paper explicitly calls it no-till
Long-term trials may show different effects in early vs late years - extract each year separately
extraction_priorities: 1. CRITICAL: Extract EVERY crop-year-site combination separately
2. Treatment = NO-TILL; Control = CONVENTIONAL TILLAGE (most intensive tillage in the study)
3. If multiple crops tested, extract EACH crop vs control
4. If reduced tillage AND no-till both present, extract no-till vs conventional (not reduced vs conventional)
5. Get variance (SE/SD/LSD) and sample size (n)
6. Record crop species and years since no-till adoption
7. Record residue management practice
topic_brief.benchmark_notes: Overall -5.7%; Wheat -2.6%; Maize -7.6%; Rice -7.5%; Soybean +0.3%; Oilseed rape -9.0%
